title: NVIDIA Software Stack, Python Tooling and Deployment

questions.q: What distinguishes Tensor Cores from general-purpose CUDA cores on an NVIDIA GPU?
options: Tensor Cores handle integer and control-flow work, while CUDA cores handle all floating-point math
Tensor Cores are specialized units that perform small matrix multiply-accumulate operations per instruction, often in reduced precision
Tensor Cores are a separate memory tier that caches tensors closer to the SMs than HBM
Tensor Cores are only used for graphics ray tracing and are idle during deep learning workloads
questions.why: Tensor Cores execute fused matrix multiply-accumulate on small tiles (e.g., FP16/BF16/FP8 inputs with higher-precision accumulation), which is exactly the GEMM work that dominates transformers. CUDA cores execute scalar/vector arithmetic per thread. Option C confuses compute units with caches; Tensor Cores are not memory.

questions.q: Which statement best describes HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) as used on data-center GPUs such as the A100 and H100?
options: It is the on-chip shared memory inside each SM, configurable per thread block
It is host system RAM that the GPU accesses over PCIe using unified memory
It is a narrow-bus, high-clock memory type mainly used on consumer gaming cards
It is stacked DRAM placed on the same package as the GPU die, connected through a very wide interface to deliver terabytes per second of bandwidth
questions.why: HBM stacks DRAM dies and places them next to the GPU on an interposer, giving a very wide bus and multi-TB/s bandwidth. Option C describes GDDR (narrower bus, higher clocks) used on most consumer cards. Shared memory (A) is a small on-chip SRAM, not HBM.

questions.q: In NVIDIA GPU architecture, what is a Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)?
options: The basic processing block that contains CUDA cores, Tensor Cores, registers, and shared memory, and onto which thread blocks are scheduled
The driver component that streams kernels from the CPU to the GPU over PCIe
A dedicated chip on the board that manages communication over NVLink
A software scheduler inside PyTorch that splits a batch across multiple GPUs
questions.why: A GPU is made of many SMs; each SM holds execution units, a register file, and shared memory/L1 cache, and the hardware assigns thread blocks to SMs. Option B sounds plausible because of the word "streaming", but it describes driver behavior, not a hardware unit.

questions.q: How many threads are in a warp, the group of threads an NVIDIA SM schedules and executes together?
questions.why: NVIDIA GPUs execute threads in warps of 32 that share an instruction stream. 64 is the "wavefront" size on some AMD GPUs, which is a common source of confusion. Thread block sizes are usually chosen as multiples of 32 for this reason.

questions.q: Which pairing of GPU and architecture is correct?
options: A100 – Hopper; H100 – Ampere
A100 – Volta; H100 – Blackwell
A100 – Ampere; H100 – Hopper
A100 – Ampere; H100 – Blackwell
questions.why: The letter in the product name follows the architecture: A100 is Ampere and H100 is Hopper. Blackwell is the following generation (e.g., B200), and Volta was the generation of the V100. Swapping the two (A) is the most common slip.

questions.q: Which GPU architecture introduced the Transformer Engine with hardware FP8 Tensor Core support?
options: Hopper
Ampere
Volta
Turing
questions.why: Hopper (H100) introduced FP8 Tensor Cores and the Transformer Engine, which manages per-layer scaling so FP8 can be used for training and inference. Ampere (A100) added TF32 and BF16 Tensor Core support, not FP8, which makes it the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: Which capability is a headline feature of the Blackwell generation relative to Hopper?
options: The first use of Tensor Cores on a data-center GPU
Replacing HBM with GDDR to reduce cost
Removing NVLink in favor of PCIe-only communication
Second-generation Transformer Engine with support for FP4 precision
questions.why: Blackwell extends the Transformer Engine with FP4 support for further throughput and memory gains in inference. Tensor Cores first appeared with Volta, so A is wrong; Blackwell data-center parts continue to use HBM and NVLink.

questions.q: What is the role of cuDNN in the deep learning stack?
options: It is a compiler that converts Python code into CUDA kernels at runtime
It is a GPU-accelerated library of primitives for deep neural networks, such as convolutions, normalization, and attention, used by frameworks like PyTorch
It is NVIDIA's library for multi-GPU collective communication
It is a container registry of pretrained deep learning models
questions.why: cuDNN provides highly tuned implementations of common neural network operations that frameworks call under the hood. Collective communication (C) is NCCL's job, and a model registry (D) describes NGC.

questions.q: During multi-GPU data-parallel training, which NVIDIA library typically performs the all-reduce that averages gradients across GPUs?
options: cuBLAS
NCCL
cuDF
TensorRT
questions.why: NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) implements all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, and broadcast over NVLink, PCIe, and InfiniBand, and is the default backend for PyTorch distributed on GPUs. cuBLAS performs the matrix math inside each GPU but does not communicate between GPUs.

questions.q: What is CUDA?
options: A file format for storing trained neural network weights
A high-level deep learning framework that competes with PyTorch
A type of GPU memory with error-correcting codes
NVIDIA's parallel computing platform and programming model, including the toolkit, compiler, and runtime used to run code on GPUs
questions.why: CUDA is the platform (language extensions, nvcc compiler, runtime and driver APIs, libraries) that everything else builds on. It is not a framework like PyTorch (B); PyTorch uses CUDA and CUDA libraries underneath.

questions.q: What does the NVIDIA NGC catalog primarily provide?
options: GPU-optimized containers, pretrained models, Helm charts, and other resources for AI and HPC workloads
A managed Kubernetes service that hosts customer clusters
A hardware procurement portal for ordering DGX systems
A benchmark leaderboard ranking LLMs by accuracy
questions.why: NGC is NVIDIA's hub of tested software: framework containers (PyTorch, NeMo, Triton), models, Helm charts, and resources, pulled from the nvcr.io registry. It is not itself a managed Kubernetes service (B); you run its artifacts on your own infrastructure or a cloud.

questions.q: What is NVIDIA AI Enterprise?
options: A free open-source fork of PyTorch maintained by NVIDIA
A specific DGX hardware model sold to enterprises
A licensed, supported software suite of NVIDIA AI frameworks, tools, and microservices (such as NIM) for production deployment
An online course required before using NVIDIA GPUs in the cloud
questions.why: NVIDIA AI Enterprise bundles production-grade, security-maintained versions of NVIDIA AI software with enterprise support and certification across platforms. It is software, not hardware (B), and it is commercially licensed rather than a free fork.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the NVIDIA NeMo framework?
options: Serving any model format over HTTP and gRPC with dynamic batching
Accelerating pandas-style dataframe operations on GPUs
Building, training, and customizing generative AI models such as LLMs, including pretraining, fine-tuning, and alignment at scale
Monitoring GPU health metrics in data centers
questions.why: NeMo is NVIDIA's framework for creating and customizing generative AI models, built on Megatron-Core for scalable parallelism. Serving (A) is Triton's role, and dataframe acceleration (B) is RAPIDS cuDF.

questions.q: What is an NVIDIA NIM?
options: A prebuilt, optimized inference microservice container that exposes a model through industry-standard APIs such as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint
A model compression algorithm that prunes attention heads
A Kubernetes scheduler extension that bin-packs GPU jobs
A Python package for tokenizing text before training
questions.why: NIM packages a model with an optimized inference engine and a standard API so it can be deployed with a single container. It is a deployment artifact, not an optimization algorithm (B) or a scheduler (C).

questions.q: What is NVIDIA Triton Inference Server?
options: A compiler that converts ONNX graphs into optimized GPU engines
A language for writing GPU kernels in Python
A training framework for distributed LLM pretraining

An open-source inference server that serves models from multiple frameworks (e.g., TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, Python) over HTTP/gRPC with features like dynamic batching and concurrent model execution
questions.why: Triton Inference Server is a multi-framework serving runtime. Option B is a trap: the OpenAI "Triton" language for writing GPU kernels is a different project that shares the name. Compiling ONNX to engines (A) is TensorRT.

questions.q: What does TensorRT do?
options: Distributes training across thousands of GPUs
Optimizes a trained network for inference, using techniques like layer fusion, precision reduction, and kernel auto-tuning, and produces a serialized engine
Provides a REST API gateway for deployed models
Stores model checkpoints in a versioned registry
questions.why: TensorRT is an inference optimizer and runtime: it takes a network (often via ONNX), fuses layers, selects precision (FP16/INT8/FP8), picks the fastest kernels for the target GPU, and serializes an engine. It does not serve requests over the network (C); Triton does that.

questions.q: Why would you choose TensorRT-LLM over plain TensorRT for serving a large decoder-only model?
options: TensorRT-LLM is the only way to run any model on NVIDIA GPUs
TensorRT-LLM adds LLM-specific features such as optimized attention kernels, paged KV cache, in-flight batching, and multi-GPU tensor parallelism
TensorRT-LLM trains models faster by using FP64 precision
TensorRT-LLM converts LLMs into CPU-only executables for edge devices
questions.why: Autoregressive generation needs KV-cache management, token-level batching, and multi-GPU sharding that general TensorRT does not provide out of the box. TensorRT-LLM is an inference library, not a training tool, and it targets GPUs rather than CPUs.

questions.q: What is NeMo Guardrails used for?
options: Preventing GPU overheating by throttling clocks
Limiting the amount of GPU memory a container can allocate
Fine-tuning a model with RLHF so that it refuses harmful requests
Adding programmable rails around an LLM application, such as keeping conversations on topic, checking inputs and outputs, and blocking jailbreak attempts
questions.why: NeMo Guardrails is a runtime toolkit that sits between the user and the LLM, with rails defined in configuration and Colang flows. It does not change model weights; RLHF (C) is a training-time alignment method, which is the tempting confusion.

questions.q: A data scientist's pandas preprocessing of a 50 GB log dataset is slow. Which RAPIDS library offers a pandas-like API on the GPU?
options: cuDF
cuML
cuGraph
cuBLAS
questions.why: cuDF provides GPU dataframes with a pandas-like API (and a cudf.pandas accelerator mode for existing pandas code). cuML is the scikit-learn-like machine learning library, which is the closest distractor, but it is not a dataframe library.

questions.q: Which directory layout is a valid Triton model repository for a TensorRT model named `llm_encoder`?
options: `models/llm_encoder.plan` with a `config.json` next to it
`models/1/llm_encoder/model.plan`
`models/llm_encoder/config.pbtxt` and `models/llm_encoder/1/model.plan`
`models/config.pbtxt` listing all models, with files in `models/weights/`
questions.why: Triton expects `<repository>/<model-name>/` containing an optional-or-required `config.pbtxt` and numeric version subdirectories holding the model file. Option B reverses the version and model-name levels, which is a frequent mistake.

questions.q: What does enabling dynamic batching in a Triton model configuration do?
options: It changes the model's batch dimension during training
It splits a large incoming batch into single requests to lower latency
It combines individual inference requests that arrive close together into one larger batch on the server to improve GPU utilization
It automatically adds more GPUs when the request rate rises
questions.why: The dynamic batcher holds requests briefly (bounded by a queue delay) and groups them, trading a little latency for much higher throughput. It does not scale hardware (D); that is the job of an autoscaler.

questions.q: By default, which ports does Triton Inference Server use for HTTP, gRPC, and Prometheus metrics?
options: 8000 (HTTP), 8001 (gRPC), 8002 (metrics)
80 (HTTP), 443 (gRPC), 9090 (metrics)
8080 (HTTP), 50051 (gRPC), 9100 (metrics)
8001 (HTTP), 8000 (gRPC), 8002 (metrics)
questions.why: Triton listens on 8000 for HTTP/REST, 8001 for gRPC, and 8002 for the Prometheus metrics endpoint. Option D swaps HTTP and gRPC; option C lists common defaults of other tools (50051 is a typical gRPC example port, 9100 is node-exporter).

questions.q:
```python
import torch
x = torch.randn(4, 4)
x.to("cuda")
y = x @ x
print(y.device)
```

What does this print?
options: `cuda:0`
It raises an error because `x` is on two devices
`cuda`
`cpu`
questions.why: For tensors, `.to()` is not in-place; it returns a new tensor on the GPU, which is discarded here. `x` stays on the CPU, so `y` is computed on the CPU. The fix is `x = x.to("cuda")`. (By contrast, `nn.Module.to()` does modify the module in place.)

questions.q: What is the main effect of wrapping inference code in `with torch.no_grad():`?
options: Dropout layers are disabled
Operations are not recorded in the autograd graph, so activations are not saved for backward, reducing memory and computation
The model's weights are frozen permanently
The model is automatically moved to the GPU
questions.why: `torch.no_grad()` turns off gradient tracking inside the block. It does not change layer behavior such as dropout or batch norm; that is what `model.eval()` controls, making A the tempting but wrong answer.

questions.q: What does `model.eval()` change in a PyTorch model?
options: It disables gradient computation for all parameters
It switches layers like dropout and batch normalization to their inference behavior
It converts the model to FP16
It compiles the model with TorchScript
questions.why: `eval()` sets `self.training = False` on every submodule, so dropout stops dropping and batch norm uses running statistics. It does not stop autograd (A); you still need `torch.no_grad()` or `torch.inference_mode()` for that.

questions.q:
```python
w = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
loss = w ** 2
loss.backward()
print(w.grad)
```

What is printed?
options: `tensor(3.)`
`tensor(9.)`
`None`
`tensor(6.)`
questions.why: `backward()` computes d(loss)/dw = 2w = 6 and stores it in `w.grad`. Option B is the loss value itself, not its gradient; `None` would appear only if backward had not been called or `requires_grad` were False.

questions.q: Which NVIDIA library supplies the GPU-accelerated dense linear algebra routines (such as GEMM) that frameworks call for the matrix multiplications inside transformer layers?
options: cuBLAS
cuDNN
NCCL
cuFFT
questions.why: cuBLAS is NVIDIA's implementation of the BLAS API, and its GEMM kernels (using Tensor Cores where possible) power the linear projections in transformers. cuDNN is the tempting distractor, but it focuses on neural-network primitives such as convolutions and normalization rather than general linear algebra.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of NVLink?
options: Connecting the CPU to system RAM at higher speed than DDR5
Linking separate data-center racks over long-distance optical fiber
Providing a high-bandwidth, low-latency direct interconnect between GPUs (and some CPUs) that is much faster than PCIe
Streaming video output from the GPU to multiple displays
questions.why: NVLink lets GPUs exchange data directly at hundreds of GB/s, which is essential for tensor parallelism and fast all-reduce inside a server. Connecting racks across a data center (B) is the job of a network such as InfiniBand or Ethernet, not NVLink.

questions.q: In an 8-GPU HGX/DGX server, what does NVSwitch add on top of NVLink?
options: It converts NVLink traffic into Ethernet packets for the data-center network
It acts as a switch fabric so every GPU can talk to every other GPU at full NVLink bandwidth simultaneously
It switches the GPU between graphics and compute modes
It partitions one GPU into several isolated instances
questions.why: Point-to-point NVLink alone limits which GPU pairs are directly connected; NVSwitch chips create an all-to-all NVLink fabric across the GPUs in the node (and, in newer systems, across racks). Partitioning a GPU (D) is MIG, a different feature.

questions.q: A team scales LLM training from one DGX node to 32 nodes. Which technology most commonly carries the gradient traffic between nodes?
options: PCIe Gen5
NVLink bridges between adjacent servers
USB4 links
InfiniBand networking with RDMA
questions.why: InfiniBand (e.g., NVIDIA Quantum switches with ConnectX adapters) gives low-latency, high-bandwidth RDMA between nodes, and NCCL uses it for inter-node collectives. PCIe connects devices inside a single server, so it cannot connect separate nodes.

questions.q: What does MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) on an A100 or H100 allow?
options: Splitting one physical GPU into up to seven isolated instances, each with its own dedicated compute and memory
Combining several GPUs into one logical GPU with pooled memory
Running the same kernel on multiple GPUs without code changes
Migrating a running process from one GPU to another without downtime
questions.why: MIG hardware-partitions SMs, L2 cache, and memory so up to seven workloads run side by side with quality-of-service isolation. Option B describes the opposite direction; MIG makes one GPU look like several, not several look like one.

questions.q: What is the difference between NVIDIA DGX and HGX?
options: DGX is for inference only; HGX is for training only
DGX uses PCIe GPUs; HGX uses consumer GeForce GPUs
DGX is NVIDIA's complete, turnkey AI system with its software stack; HGX is the GPU baseboard platform that server partners build their own systems around
DGX is a cloud service; HGX is the on-premises version of the same service
questions.why: HGX provides the multi-GPU board with NVLink/NVSwitch that OEMs integrate into their servers, while DGX is NVIDIA's own fully integrated system (plus DGX software and support). Both are used for training and inference, so A is a false split.

questions.q: An engineer wants a quick look at each GPU's memory usage, utilization, temperature, and the processes running on it from a shell. Which tool should they use?
options: `nvcc --version`
`nvidia-smi`
`nsys profile`
`lspci`
questions.why: `nvidia-smi` reports per-GPU memory used/total, GPU utilization, temperature, power, and the processes holding GPU memory. `nvcc --version` only reports the installed CUDA compiler version, and `nsys` records a detailed profile rather than giving a status snapshot.

questions.q: A developer runs `docker run nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:<tag> python -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())"` and gets `False` on a host with working GPUs. What is the most likely fix?
options: Install CUDA inside the container image again
Rebuild PyTorch from source inside the container
Use a CPU-only base image
Install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit on the host and pass `--gpus all` to `docker run`
questions.why: Containers do not see GPUs by default; the NVIDIA Container Toolkit plus the `--gpus` flag injects the devices and host driver libraries. NGC containers already ship the CUDA user-space libraries, so reinstalling CUDA inside (A) does not address the missing device access.

questions.q: How does a Kubernetes pod request one NVIDIA GPU when the NVIDIA device plugin is installed?
options: `resources.limits: {nvidia.com/gpu: 1}`
`resources.limits: {cpu: "gpu-1"}`
`nodeSelector: {gpu: "true"}` alone
`env: [{name: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES, value: "0"}]` alone
questions.why: The device plugin advertises `nvidia.com/gpu` as an extended resource, and the scheduler places the pod only on a node with a free GPU. Setting `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` (D) does nothing for scheduling and does not grant the container access to the device.

questions.q: What does the NVIDIA GPU Operator do in a Kubernetes cluster?
options: It serves LLMs behind an OpenAI-compatible API
It automates deployment and management of the GPU software stack on nodes, such as the driver, container toolkit, device plugin, and monitoring
It schedules training jobs across multiple clusters by priority
It compiles models into TensorRT engines when pods start
questions.why: The GPU Operator uses the operator pattern to install and lifecycle-manage the components needed to run GPU workloads, so nodes do not have to be hand-configured. Serving models (A) is what NIM or Triton do once the nodes are GPU-ready.

questions.q: Which NVIDIA tool records a system-wide timeline of CPU threads, CUDA API calls, kernel launches, and memory copies to find where an application spends time?
options: Nsight Compute
DCGM
Nsight Systems (`nsys`)
`nvidia-smi dmon`
questions.why: Nsight Systems is the starting point for performance analysis because it shows the whole application timeline, including CPU/GPU overlap and idle gaps. Nsight Compute is the tempting choice, but it profiles individual kernels in depth rather than the whole system.

questions.q: What is ONNX?
options: An NVIDIA-only binary format for TensorRT engines
A Python library for loading datasets from the Hugging Face Hub
A GPU driver API used by containers
An open, framework-neutral format for representing trained models as a graph of standard operators
questions.why: ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) lets a model exported from PyTorch or another framework be consumed by runtimes such as ONNX Runtime or TensorRT. A TensorRT engine (A) is a different, hardware-specific serialized artifact.

questions.q:
```python
from transformers import pipeline
clf = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")
print(clf("The deployment went smoothly."))
```

What does `pipeline()` provide here?
options: A training loop that fine-tunes a model on the given sentence
A high-level inference wrapper that bundles a default model, its tokenizer, preprocessing, and postprocessing for the task
A Triton ensemble that runs on a remote server
A data pipeline that streams a dataset from the Hub
questions.why: `pipeline(task)` loads a suitable model and tokenizer and handles tokenization and output formatting, returning e.g. a label and score. It runs locally and performs inference only; it does not train (A).

questions.q: Which call loads a dataset from the Hugging Face Hub as an Arrow-backed `Dataset`/`DatasetDict` object?
options: `AutoDataset.from_pretrained("imdb")`
`torch.utils.data.load("imdb")`
`datasets.load_dataset("imdb")`
`transformers.pipeline("imdb")`
questions.why: `load_dataset` from the `datasets` library downloads and caches the data in Apache Arrow format, with memory-mapping and methods like `map` and `filter`. `AutoDataset.from_pretrained` (A) imitates the transformers naming style but does not exist.

questions.q: A developer wants to load a pretrained decoder-only model and its matching tokenizer for text generation. Which pair of classes is most appropriate?
options: `AutoTokenizer` and `AutoModelForCausalLM`
`AutoTokenizer` and `AutoModelForSequenceClassification`
`AutoFeatureExtractor` and `AutoModel`
`AutoConfig` and `AutoModelForMaskedLM`
questions.why: `AutoModelForCausalLM` adds the language-modeling head needed for next-token prediction and supports `generate()`. `AutoModelForSequenceClassification` (B) attaches a classification head instead, and `AutoModelForMaskedLM` (D) is for BERT-style masked models.

questions.q: What is the role of `torch.utils.data.DataLoader`?
options: It defines how to fetch a single sample by index
It moves the model's parameters to the GPU
It saves checkpoints during training
It wraps a Dataset to produce batches, with optional shuffling, collation, and parallel loading through worker processes
questions.why: The `Dataset` defines `__len__` and `__getitem__` for a single sample (A); the `DataLoader` iterates over it to build batches using `batch_size`, `shuffle`, `collate_fn`, and `num_workers`. Confusing the two is a common beginner mistake.

options: `(512, 10)`; `forward` cannot be called directly
`(8, 10)`; calling the module runs `__call__`, which invokes `forward` along with any registered hooks
`(8, 512)`; calling the module skips the linear layer during the first pass
`(10,)`; calling the module averages over the batch
questions.why: A `Linear(512, 10)` maps each of the 8 input rows to 10 outputs. Calling `forward` directly does work, so A is wrong, but it bypasses hooks, which is why the idiomatic form is `module(x)`.

questions.q: Why does a typical PyTorch training loop call `optimizer.zero_grad()` each iteration?
options: Because `backward()` accumulates (adds) into `.grad`, so old gradients would otherwise be summed with new ones
Because it resets the weights to their initial values
Because it frees the activations saved for the backward pass
Because it lowers the learning rate when the loss plateaus
questions.why: PyTorch accumulates gradients by design, which enables gradient accumulation across micro-batches but requires explicit clearing each step. It does not touch weights (B) or the learning-rate schedule (D).

questions.q: Which line is the standard way to write PyTorch code that uses a GPU when available and falls back to the CPU otherwise?
options: `device = torch.device("gpu")`
`device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.device_count() > 8 else "cpu"`
`device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")`
`device = torch.cuda.current_device()` on every machine
questions.why: `torch.cuda.is_available()` checks for a usable CUDA device and driver. `"gpu"` (A) is not a valid PyTorch device string, and `current_device()` (D) raises an error on a machine without CUDA.

questions.q: A robotics team needs to run a small vision-language model on a battery-powered robot without network connectivity. Which NVIDIA platform is designed for this?
options: DGX H100
NVIDIA Jetson (e.g., Jetson Orin)
HGX B200
NVIDIA AI Enterprise on a cloud VM
questions.why: Jetson modules are compact, power-efficient embedded computers with an integrated GPU, built for edge AI in robots and devices. DGX and HGX are data-center systems requiring rack power and cooling, and a cloud VM (D) fails the no-connectivity requirement.

questions.q: In model serving, what is the difference between latency and throughput?
options: Latency is total requests served per day; throughput is the GPU clock speed
They are two names for the same metric
Latency is measured only on CPUs; throughput only on GPUs
Latency is the time to complete one request; throughput is how much work (requests or tokens) the system completes per unit time
questions.why: The two often trade off: larger batches raise throughput but make individual requests wait longer. Treating them as the same metric (B) hides that trade-off, which is central to setting serving SLOs.

questions.q: A chat product's users complain that the assistant "takes too long to start answering," even though total response time is acceptable. Which serving metric best captures this complaint?
options: Time to first token (TTFT)
Tokens per second across the whole cluster
GPU memory utilization
Model parameter count
questions.why: TTFT measures the delay between sending a request and receiving the first generated token, which dominates perceived responsiveness when output is streamed. Aggregate cluster throughput (B) can be excellent while individual users still wait a long time for the first token.

questions.q: An OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint is called with `"stream": true`. How are tokens typically delivered to the client?
options: As a single JSON body after generation finishes
As a ZIP archive containing one file per token
As Server-Sent Events, with incremental `data:` chunks sent as tokens are generated
Through a separate polling endpoint the client must call every second
questions.why: OpenAI-style streaming keeps the HTTP response open and pushes `data: {...}` chunks over SSE, ending with `data: [DONE]`. Returning one JSON body (A) is the non-streaming behavior.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes gRPC compared with a typical JSON REST API?
options: gRPC can only be used from web browsers
gRPC uses HTTP/2 and binary Protocol Buffers, which typically gives lower overhead and supports bidirectional streaming
gRPC sends data as plain-text XML over HTTP/1.0
gRPC cannot carry tensors, so it is unsuitable for inference servers
questions.why: Binary serialization and HTTP/2 multiplexing make gRPC efficient for service-to-service calls, which is why Triton exposes a gRPC endpoint alongside HTTP. Browser support is actually the weak spot of gRPC (it needs gRPC-Web), so A is backwards.

questions.q: What is a canary deployment of a new model version?
options: Routing a small percentage of production traffic to the new version, watching its metrics, and increasing traffic only if it performs well
Deploying the new version to all users at once during a maintenance window
Running the new version only on synthetic test data before release
Keeping the old version's weights as a backup file on disk
questions.why: A canary exposes a limited share of real users to the new model so problems surface with small blast radius before full rollout. Switching everyone at once (B) is the risk the canary pattern is designed to avoid.

questions.q: Which RAPIDS library offers GPU-accelerated machine learning algorithms (such as k-means, random forests, and UMAP) with a scikit-learn-like API?
options: cuDF
cuGraph
cuSPARSE
cuML
questions.why: cuML mirrors much of the scikit-learn API so existing ML code can move to the GPU with few changes, which is useful for tasks such as clustering embeddings. cuDF (A) handles dataframes rather than ML algorithms, and cuGraph handles graph analytics.

questions.q:
```
name: "classifier"
platform: "onnxruntime_onnx"
max_batch_size: 32
input [ { name: "input_ids" data_type: TYPE_INT64 dims: [ -1 ] } ]
output [ { name: "logits" data_type: TYPE_FP32 dims: [ 3 ] } ]
```

What full input tensor shape does this Triton model accept?
options: `[32, -1]` only, exactly 32 rows every time
`[-1]`, a single sequence with no batch dimension
`[batch, seq_len]` with batch from 1 to 32 and variable sequence length
`[batch, 3]` with batch up to 32
questions.why: When `max_batch_size > 0`, Triton prepends an implicit batch dimension that is not listed in `dims`, so `dims: [-1]` means one variable-length axis per item. The batch can be any size up to 32, so A is wrong; `[3]` describes the output logits, not the input.

questions.q:
```
instance_group [ { count: 2  kind: KIND_GPU  gpus: [ 0 ] } ]
```

What effect does this Triton setting have?
options: It loads two copies of the model on GPU 0 so two requests (or batches) can execute concurrently
It splits the model's layers across two GPUs
It limits the model to two requests per second
It creates two versions of the model for A/B testing
questions.why: `instance_group` controls how many execution instances of the model exist and where; two instances on one GPU can overlap work and improve utilization for small models. It does not shard layers across GPUs (B), which would be model parallelism inside the backend.

questions.q: An ML engineer raises `max_queue_delay_microseconds` in Triton's `dynamic_batching` block from 100 to 5000. Under moderate, steady traffic, what is the most likely outcome?
options: Lower latency and lower throughput
Larger average batches and higher throughput, at the cost of higher per-request latency
No change, because the setting only affects CPU models
Requests start being rejected with timeout errors
questions.why: The queue delay is how long the batcher may wait to collect more requests; waiting longer forms bigger batches but adds up to that delay to each request. Option A reverses the trade-off.

questions.q: A pipeline needs tokenization (Python), a TensorRT encoder, and a postprocessing step, and the team wants clients to make a single call without intermediate tensors crossing the network. Which Triton feature fits?
options: Model warmup
Rate limiter
Explicit model control mode
An ensemble model that chains the three models as steps in one DAG
questions.why: An ensemble's `config.pbtxt` maps the outputs of one model to the inputs of the next, so Triton executes the whole pipeline server-side for one client request. Explicit model control (C) only governs which models are loaded, not how they are chained.

questions.q: A team needs custom Python preprocessing (regex cleanup and tokenization) to run inside Triton next to their models. Which backend should they use?
options: TensorRT backend
ONNX Runtime backend
Python backend, implementing a `TritonPythonModel` class with an `execute` method
FIL backend
questions.why: The Python backend runs arbitrary Python code in a `model.py` that defines `TritonPythonModel` (with `initialize`, `execute`, `finalize`). The FIL backend serves tree-based models such as XGBoost, so it does not run arbitrary preprocessing code.

questions.q: Which Triton backend serves TensorRT-LLM engines with in-flight batching and paged KV cache support?
options: The TensorRT-LLM backend (`tensorrtllm`)
The standard TensorRT backend (`tensorrt_plan`)
The PyTorch (LibTorch) backend
The OpenVINO backend
questions.why: The dedicated TensorRT-LLM backend wraps the TensorRT-LLM runtime and its batch manager, providing in-flight batching and KV-cache management. The plain TensorRT backend (B) runs ordinary TensorRT engines and lacks the LLM-specific scheduling.

questions.q: A Triton model directory contains version folders `1/`, `2/`, and `3/`, and `config.pbtxt` sets no `version_policy`. Which versions are served?
options: All three versions
Only version 1
Only version 3, the highest-numbered
None until a version is chosen explicitly
questions.why: The default version policy is `latest { num_versions: 1 }`, so Triton loads only the highest version number. To serve several versions side by side you set `version_policy: { all {} }` or `{ specific { versions: [...] } }`, which is why A is tempting but wrong for the default.

questions.q: Triton's metrics show queue time per request climbing sharply while compute time per inference stays flat, and the GPU has spare memory and is not fully busy. What is the most reasonable first change?
options: Lower `max_batch_size` to 1
Add model instances (`instance_group` count) or enable/tune dynamic batching
Switch the client from gRPC to HTTP
Retrain the model with fewer layers
questions.why: Rising queue time with constant compute time means requests are waiting for a free execution slot, not running slower. More instances or better batching increase concurrency on the under-used GPU; shrinking the batch (A) would make queuing worse.

questions.q: A Kubernetes deployment of Triton should send traffic to a pod only after its models are loaded. Which endpoint is the best readiness probe?
options: `GET /v2/health/ready` on port 8000
`GET /metrics` on port 8002
`GET /v2/health/live` on port 8000
A TCP check on port 8001
questions.why: The KServe-v2 readiness endpoint returns success only when the server is ready to handle inference requests. `/v2/health/live` (C) only shows the process is alive and is suited to a liveness probe; an open TCP port can exist while models are still loading.

questions.q: An engine built with TensorRT on an A100 fails to load on an H100 node running the same container. What is the most likely explanation?
options: TensorRT engines can only run on the GPU serial number they were built on
The ONNX file was corrupted during copying
H100 does not support FP16
TensorRT engines are specialized to the GPU architecture (and TensorRT version) they were built for, so the engine must be rebuilt on the target hardware
questions.why: TensorRT selects and tunes kernels for the specific GPU during the build, so engines are not portable across architectures by default. The restriction is per architecture and version, not per physical device (A).

questions.q: When converting a model to INT8 with TensorRT using post-training quantization, why is a calibration dataset needed?
options: To fine-tune the weights with gradient descent
To estimate activation value ranges so suitable scale factors can be chosen for INT8
To check that the ONNX graph has no unsupported operators
To measure the accuracy of the FP32 baseline
questions.why: INT8 represents values with a scale factor, and activation ranges depend on real inputs, so representative samples are run through the network to collect statistics. No weight training happens during post-training calibration, which rules out A.

questions.q: Why does in-flight (continuous) batching in TensorRT-LLM improve GPU utilization over static batching for chat workloads?
options: It pads all requests to the same output length so kernels are uniform
It waits until a full batch of identical prompts arrives
Finished sequences leave the batch and new requests join at each generation step, instead of the whole batch waiting for its longest sequence
It runs each request on a separate GPU
questions.why: Output lengths vary widely, so static batches leave slots idle once short responses finish. In-flight batching schedules at the iteration level and refills those slots immediately; padding everything (A) is exactly the waste it avoids.

questions.q: Put the typical TensorRT-LLM deployment steps for a Hugging Face model in order.
options: Build engine → convert checkpoint → download weights → serve
Download HF weights → convert to a TensorRT-LLM checkpoint (optionally quantizing) → build the engine with `trtllm-build` → serve (e.g., via Triton)
Serve the HF weights → profile → convert checkpoint → build engine
Download weights → build engine → convert checkpoint → serve
questions.why: The engine builder consumes a TensorRT-LLM checkpoint, so conversion (and quantization, if used) must come before the build. Option D builds before converting, which is impossible because the builder has nothing in its format to consume. (Newer TensorRT-LLM releases also offer a higher-level LLM API that automates these steps.)

questions.q: A 70B-parameter model in FP16 needs about 140 GB for weights alone, and each GPU in the node has 80 GB with NVLink. Which TensorRT-LLM setting lets the model be served from that node?
options: Tensor parallelism of 2 or more, sharding each layer's weights across GPUs
Increasing `max_batch_size`
Data parallelism with a full model copy per GPU
Enabling streaming output
questions.why: Tensor parallelism splits weight matrices so each GPU holds a fraction of the model; TP=2 gives about 70 GB of weights per GPU, and TP=4 or 8 leaves more room for KV cache. Data parallelism (C) replicates the full 140 GB on each GPU, so it cannot fit.

questions.q: A developer has code that uses the `openai` Python client and wants to point it at a locally deployed LLM NIM. What is the minimal change?
options: Rewrite the code to use Triton's gRPC client
Convert prompts to protobuf messages
Install NeMo and call `nemo.generate()`
Set the client's `base_url` to the NIM endpoint (e.g., `http://localhost:8000/v1`) and use the NIM's model name
questions.why: LLM NIMs expose OpenAI-compatible routes such as `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/models`, so existing OpenAI client code works after changing the base URL and model name. Rewriting to a Triton client (A) is unnecessary work.

questions.q: When an LLM NIM container starts on a given GPU type, how does it achieve good performance without the user building engines?
options: It compiles CUDA kernels from source on every request
It always runs the unoptimized Hugging Face model in FP32
It selects a prebuilt optimized profile (engine and settings) matching the detected GPU and configuration, falling back to a generic backend when none matches
It asks the user to upload a TensorRT engine at startup
questions.why: NIM packages optimized model profiles for supported GPUs and tensor-parallel layouts and chooses one automatically at startup. Running FP32 Hugging Face code (B) would discard the main value of NIM, which is optimized inference out of the box.

questions.q: A `docker run` of a NIM image from `nvcr.io` fails with an authorization error while downloading the model. What is most likely missing?
options: An NGC API key (e.g., `docker login nvcr.io` and the `NGC_API_KEY` environment variable passed to the container)
A Hugging Face Hub token
A Kubernetes service account
A CUDA toolkit installed on the host
questions.why: NIM images live in NGC's registry, and the container uses the NGC API key to authenticate and fetch model assets. A full CUDA toolkit on the host (D) is not required; only the driver and container toolkit are.

questions.q: Which situation is a better fit for building directly on Triton Inference Server than for using a prebuilt LLM NIM?
options: Quickly deploying a popular open LLM behind an OpenAI-compatible API
Serving a custom pipeline that mixes an ONNX vision model, a Python preprocessing step, and an XGBoost model in one ensemble
Avoiding the work of building TensorRT-LLM engines for a supported model
Getting a supported, enterprise-maintained container for a standard model
questions.why: Triton's multi-backend support and ensembles suit custom, heterogeneous pipelines. Options A, C, and D describe exactly what NIM is designed for: packaged, optimized, supported models with a standard API.

questions.q: Approximately how much GPU memory do the weights alone of a 13B-parameter model need in BF16?
options: 13 GB
52 GB
6.5 GB
26 GB
questions.why: BF16 uses 2 bytes per parameter, so 13 × 10⁹ × 2 bytes ≈ 26 GB. 52 GB (B) is the FP32 figure, and 13 GB (A) would be INT8; real deployments also need extra memory for the KV cache and activations.

questions.q: A team quantizes an 8B-parameter model to 4-bit weights. Ignoring scale-factor overhead, roughly how large are the weights?
options: 4 GB
8 GB
16 GB
32 GB
questions.why: 4 bits is half a byte, so 8 × 10⁹ × 0.5 bytes = 4 GB. 8 GB (B) is the INT8 size, and 16 GB is the FP16 size; small extra overhead comes from per-group scales.

questions.q: A platform team runs dozens of small models (each needing under 10 GB) for different internal tenants and must guarantee that one tenant's load cannot slow another's or read its memory. What is the best approach on A100/H100 GPUs?
options: Run all models in one process on a full GPU
Use NVLink to pool the GPUs
Partition GPUs with MIG and assign isolated instances to tenants
Use tensor parallelism across all GPUs
questions.why: MIG gives each instance dedicated SMs, cache, and memory, providing performance and fault isolation for small workloads that would waste a whole GPU. Sharing one process (A) offers no isolation, and tensor parallelism solves models too large for one GPU, the opposite problem.

questions.q: `nvidia-smi` reports 100% GPU-Util during inference, yet profiling shows throughput far below the GPU's capability. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The GPU is saturated and only a faster GPU can help
GPU-Util measures memory bandwidth used, so memory is the bottleneck
GPU-Util is the temperature-scaled clock speed
GPU-Util is the share of time at least one kernel was running, so small kernels using few SMs can still show 100%
questions.why: The metric samples whether the GPU was busy, not how much of its compute was used, so it overstates saturation for small batches. Tools such as Nsight Systems/Compute or DCGM's SM activity metrics reveal actual occupancy; concluding the GPU is maxed out (A) is the common mistake.

questions.q: A developer's inference script fails with "CUDA out of memory" even though the model should fit. `nvidia-smi` shows another Python process holding 60 GB on the same GPU. What should they do first?
options: Quantize the model to INT4
Stop the stale process (or select a different GPU) so the memory is freed
Increase the batch size to use memory more efficiently
Reinstall the NVIDIA driver
questions.why: The processes section of `nvidia-smi` shows which PIDs hold memory; a leftover notebook kernel or crashed job is a frequent cause. Quantizing (A) treats a symptom and may be unnecessary once the real cause is removed.

questions.q:
```python
scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler()
with torch.autocast(device_type="cuda", dtype=torch.float16):
    loss = model(x).loss
scaler.scale(loss).backward()
scaler.step(optimizer); scaler.update()
```

Why is a `GradScaler` used here, and when could it be dropped?
options: It scales the loss to prevent FP16 gradient underflow; it is usually unnecessary with `dtype=torch.bfloat16` because BF16 has the same exponent range as FP32
It speeds up the optimizer; it can be dropped on Hopper GPUs
It clips gradients to norm 1.0; it can be dropped when using Adam
It converts weights to FP16 permanently; it can be dropped at inference
questions.why: FP16 has a narrow exponent range, so small gradients can flush to zero; scaling the loss up and unscaling before the step avoids this. BF16 trades mantissa bits for FP32's exponent range, so loss scaling is normally not needed. GradScaler does not clip gradients (C).

questions.q: What does wrapping a model with `torch.compile(model)` do?
options: Exports the model to ONNX for use in other runtimes
Converts the model to INT8 automatically
Captures the model's Python operations into graphs and generates optimized fused kernels, with compilation happening on the first calls
Distributes the model across all available GPUs
questions.why: `torch.compile` uses TorchDynamo to capture graphs and a backend (TorchInductor by default) to generate fused kernels, keeping normal PyTorch usage. It is not an exporter (A) or a quantizer (B), and the first calls are slower because they trigger compilation.

questions.q: How does `torch.inference_mode()` differ from `torch.no_grad()`?
options: It also switches dropout off, so `model.eval()` is not needed
It disables gradient tracking and additionally skips autograd bookkeeping such as version counters, making it slightly faster, but its tensors cannot later be used in autograd
It runs the model on the CPU to save GPU memory
It is deprecated and identical to `no_grad()`
questions.why: `inference_mode` is a stricter no-grad mode intended for pure inference. Like `no_grad`, it does not change layer behavior, so you still call `model.eval()` for dropout and batch norm, making A wrong.

questions.q: During training, Nsight Systems shows long GPU idle gaps while the main CPU thread is busy decoding and augmenting each batch. Which change most directly helps?
options: Reduce the model's hidden size
Switch the optimizer from AdamW to SGD
Increase `torch.backends.cudnn` precision
Set `num_workers > 0` (and `pin_memory=True`) on the DataLoader so batches are prepared in parallel
questions.why: The GPU is waiting on input preparation, a CPU bottleneck, so loading in worker processes and using pinned memory for faster host-to-device copies overlaps data prep with compute. Shrinking the model (A) would only make the GPU idle for an even larger fraction of time.

questions.q:
```python
model = MyModel().to("cuda")
batch = tokenizer(texts, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)
out = model(**batch)
```

This raises "Expected all tensors to be on the same device." What is the fix?
options: Call `model.cpu()` before `.to("cuda")`
Wrap the call in `torch.no_grad()`
Move the inputs too, e.g., `batch = {k: v.to("cuda") for k, v in batch.items()}`
Set `padding=False`
questions.why: The tokenizer returns CPU tensors, but the model's weights live on the GPU, and PyTorch does not move data implicitly. `no_grad` (B) changes autograd behavior, not device placement. (The returned `BatchEncoding` also supports `batch.to("cuda")`.)

questions.q: What problem does the Hugging Face `accelerate` library primarily solve?
options: Running the same PyTorch training loop on CPU, one GPU, multiple GPUs, or multiple nodes (with options like mixed precision) with minimal code changes
Converting models to TensorRT engines
Hosting models on the Hugging Face Hub
Tokenizing text faster with Rust
questions.why: `Accelerator.prepare()` wraps the model, optimizer, and dataloaders for the configured distributed setup. Fast Rust-based tokenization (D) is the `tokenizers` library, a different package.

questions.q:
```python
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "some-org/llm-34b", torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")
```

On a machine with two 48 GB GPUs, what does `device_map="auto"` do?
options: Replicates the full model on each GPU for data parallelism
Places different layers on different GPUs (spilling to CPU if needed) so the model fits, running them sequentially
Applies tensor parallelism with NCCL all-reduce in every layer
Quantizes the model to INT8 to fit on one GPU
questions.why: Accelerate's big-model inference assigns whole layers to devices based on available memory, which fits the model but leaves only one GPU active at a time. It is not tensor parallelism (C), which is why dedicated serving engines are faster for multi-GPU LLM inference.

questions.q: The first few requests after a Triton model loads are much slower than later ones, triggering latency alerts after every deployment. Which Triton feature addresses this?
options: Setting max_batch_size to 0
Disabling the metrics endpoint
Using the version policy "latest"
Configuring model_warmup in config.pbtxt
questions.why: model_warmup sends synthetic requests while the model loads, so lazy initialization (memory allocation, kernel selection, graph capture) finishes before the model reports ready. max_batch_size 0 only changes how the batch dimension is declared and does nothing for cold-start latency.

questions.q:
```python
torch.onnx.export(model, (input_ids,), "model.onnx",
                  input_names=["input_ids"], output_names=["logits"])
```

The example `input_ids` had shape `(1, 16)`. In production, inputs with batch 4 and length 50 fail. What was missing?
options: `opset_version=7`
`do_constant_folding=False`
`dynamic_axes` marking the batch and sequence dimensions as variable
`export_params=False`
questions.why: Without `dynamic_axes`, the exporter fixes input shapes to those of the example input. Passing e.g. `dynamic_axes={"input_ids": {0: "batch", 1: "seq"}, "logits": {0: "batch", 1: "seq"}}` keeps them symbolic. Disabling `export_params` (D) would omit the weights from the file, making things worse.

questions.q: Which command-line tool ships with TensorRT and can build an engine from an ONNX file and benchmark it?
options: `trtexec`
`nvcc`
`tritonserver`
`nsys`
questions.why: `trtexec --onnx=model.onnx --saveEngine=model.plan --fp16` parses the ONNX graph, builds an engine, and reports latency and throughput. `tritonserver` (C) serves an already-built engine rather than building one.

questions.q: A team wants a Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale inference pods on a GPU metric. Which pipeline is typical?
options: Kubelet reports GPU utilization natively to the HPA with no extra components
DCGM Exporter exposes GPU metrics to Prometheus, and a Prometheus Adapter makes them available to the HPA as custom metrics
`nvidia-smi` runs as a cron job and edits the deployment's replica count
The NVIDIA device plugin scales pods based on GPU temperature
questions.why: The built-in HPA understands CPU and memory; GPU metrics have to come through the custom-metrics API, commonly via DCGM Exporter → Prometheus → adapter. The device plugin (D) only advertises GPUs for scheduling and does no scaling.

questions.q: What is NVIDIA DCGM (Data Center GPU Manager) used for?
options: Building TensorRT engines in CI pipelines
Splitting datasets across GPUs during training
Hosting containers in the NGC registry
Monitoring, health-checking, and diagnosing GPUs across a cluster, including exporting telemetry such as utilization, memory, power, and errors
questions.why: DCGM provides fleet-level GPU telemetry, policies, and diagnostics, and DCGM Exporter publishes its metrics for Prometheus. It is an operations tool and does not build engines (A).

questions.q: An engineer sets `nvidia.com/gpu: 0.5` in a pod spec to let two small services share one GPU, and the pod is rejected. What should they do instead?
options: Use `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` for both pods and rely on the scheduler to pack them
Set `cpu: 0.5` instead
Configure GPU sharing through MIG partitions or the device plugin's time-slicing so each pod requests a whole (shared or partitioned) resource unit
Remove the GPU request and set `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0`
questions.why: `nvidia.com/gpu` is an integer extended resource, so fractions are invalid. MIG exposes partitions as separate resources and time-slicing advertises replicas of a GPU; either lets pods request whole units. With option A each pod reserves a whole GPU, so the scheduler cannot place both on one GPU.

questions.q: An LLM pod takes 6 minutes to download and load weights, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it before it becomes ready. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Add a startup probe (or longer initial delay) so liveness checks begin only after loading finishes, and cache weights on a persistent volume
Remove the readiness probe so traffic is sent immediately
Lower the pod's memory limit
Switch the service to gRPC
questions.why: Liveness probes that fire during a long load kill the container, creating a restart loop; a startup probe defers them. Removing readiness (B) would stop the restarts only by sending traffic to a pod that cannot serve it yet.

questions.q: What distinguishes a blue-green deployment from a canary deployment?
options: Blue-green tests only on synthetic traffic
Blue-green keeps two full environments and switches all traffic from old to new at once, allowing instant rollback by switching back
Blue-green requires two different model architectures
Blue-green gradually ramps traffic from 1% to 100%
questions.why: Blue-green runs the old (blue) and new (green) stacks side by side and flips the router, which is simple but exposes all users at once. Gradual ramping (D) is the defining feature of a canary, the tempting confusion.

questions.q: A team wants to compare a new model's latency and outputs on real production requests without affecting any user. Which rollout pattern fits?
options: Canary at 50%
Blue-green switch
Rolling update
Shadow (mirrored) deployment, where copies of live requests go to the new model and its responses are logged but not returned
questions.why: Shadowing measures behavior on real traffic with zero user impact, at the cost of extra compute. Any canary percentage (A) still serves some users from the new model.

questions.q: A service's latency report shows p50 = 300 ms and p99 = 4.5 s. What does p99 = 4.5 s mean?
options: The average latency is 4.5 s
99% of requests took longer than 4.5 s
99% of requests completed within 4.5 s, while the slowest 1% took longer
The maximum latency observed was 4.5 s
questions.why: The 99th percentile is the value below which 99% of observations fall, so it describes tail latency. It is not the maximum (D); the worst requests can be even slower. A large gap between p50 and p99 often points to queuing or very long generations.

questions.q: A GPU instance costs $4.00 per hour and sustains 2,000 output tokens/s at full load. Approximately what is the cost per 1 million output tokens?
options: About $0.56
About $2.00
About $0.07
About $5.60
questions.why: One hour produces 2,000 × 3,600 = 7.2 million tokens, so $4.00 / 7.2 ≈ $0.56 per million. Option D is off by a factor of ten, a typical unit slip; real costs are higher if the GPU is not fully loaded.

questions.q: Load testing shows one LLM replica handles 12 requests/s while meeting the latency SLO. Peak traffic is expected at 100 requests/s, and the team wants about 20% headroom. How many replicas should they plan for?
questions.why: 100 × 1.2 = 120 requests/s, and 120 / 12 = 10 replicas. 9 replicas (B) is enough for the raw 100 requests/s (100 / 12 ≈ 8.3, rounded up) but leaves less than the requested headroom.

questions.q: An LLM service receives 20 requests/s and each request takes on average 3 s from arrival to completion. By Little's law, about how many requests are in the system at any moment?
questions.why: Little's law says L = λ × W = 20 requests/s × 3 s = 60 concurrent requests, which informs batch-size and KV-cache capacity planning. 6.7 (A) comes from dividing instead of multiplying.

questions.q: Which requirement most strongly favors deploying an LLM on an edge device such as Jetson rather than calling a cloud endpoint?
options: Serving the largest available model at maximum quality
Handling sudden traffic spikes from millions of users
Strict data locality with intermittent connectivity and tight local latency limits
Frequent model updates several times per day
questions.why: Edge deployment keeps data on device and works offline with no network round trip, at the cost of running smaller, usually quantized models. Serving the largest models (A) and absorbing huge traffic spikes (B) are strengths of the cloud.

questions.q: A container built on a recent CUDA version fails on a host with an old NVIDIA driver, reporting that the driver is insufficient for the CUDA runtime. Where must the fix happen?
options: Upgrade the host's NVIDIA driver (or use an image built for an older CUDA version)
Install a newer CUDA toolkit inside the container
Reinstall PyTorch with pip inside the container
Add `--privileged` to `docker run`
questions.why: The kernel driver comes from the host and is shared into the container, while the CUDA runtime libraries live in the image; a newer runtime needs a sufficiently new driver (forward-compatibility packages help only on some data-center setups). Putting an even newer toolkit in the container (B) widens the mismatch.

questions.q: Nsight Systems shows one custom attention kernel taking 40% of step time. Which tool should the engineer use next to see that kernel's occupancy, memory throughput, and stall reasons?
options: `nvidia-smi`
Nsight Compute (`ncu`)
DCGM Exporter
Nsight Systems again with a longer capture
questions.why: The usual workflow is Nsight Systems to find the hotspot, then Nsight Compute for a detailed per-kernel analysis with hardware counters. A longer Nsight Systems capture (D) still only shows timing, not why the kernel is slow.

questions.q: A Python script sends 500 independent prompts one at a time to an LLM endpoint, and the GPU server sits mostly idle. Which client-side change best increases throughput?
options: Lower max_tokens to 1
Request XML responses instead of JSON
Send requests concurrently, e.g., with an async client and asyncio.gather under a concurrency limit
Restart the server between requests
questions.why: The client is I/O-bound, so issuing requests concurrently lets the server batch them (continuous batching) and use the GPU fully; a semaphore keeps concurrency from overloading the server. Shrinking max_tokens would make the responses useless rather than improve real throughput.

questions.q: A team building a RAG application on NVIDIA's stack wants GPU-optimized embedding and reranking models delivered as microservices. What should they use?
options: NeMo Curator
cuGraph
TensorRT Model Optimizer
NeMo Retriever microservices (embedding and reranking NIMs)
questions.why: NeMo Retriever packages embedding and reranking models as NIM microservices for building retrieval pipelines. cuGraph (B) does graph analytics and does not produce text embeddings.

questions.q: Where does NeMo Guardrails typically sit in a deployed LLM application, and what is a cost of adding it?
options: Between the application and the LLM endpoint (e.g., a NIM), checking inputs and outputs; it adds latency, especially when rails make extra LLM calls
Inside the GPU driver; it reduces memory bandwidth
In the training loop; it increases training time only
In the Kubernetes scheduler; it delays pod placement
questions.why: Guardrails runs as a runtime layer (library or server) that intercepts conversation turns. Rails such as self-check input/output or topical flows can call an LLM themselves, so latency budgets must include them. It does not run at training time (C).

questions.q: A backend microservice calls an inference server thousands of times per second with large tensor inputs, while a browser front end calls a separate public chat API. Which protocol choice is most sensible?
options: REST for the microservice, gRPC for the browser
gRPC between the microservice and the inference server, and REST/JSON (with SSE streaming) for the browser-facing API
gRPC for both
FTP for tensors, REST for chat
questions.why: gRPC's binary encoding and HTTP/2 multiplexing suit high-volume internal calls, while browsers natively speak HTTP/JSON and SSE. Option A swaps the two, putting the protocol with weak browser support in front of browsers.

questions.q: During a migration, clients must be able to call both version 2 and version 3 of a Triton model explicitly. Which configuration achieves this?
options: `version_policy: { latest: { num_versions: 1 } }`
Create two separate model repositories on two servers
`version_policy: { specific: { versions: [2, 3] } }`, with clients putting the version in the request URL
Rename version folder `2/` to `3b/`
questions.why: With a specific (or `all`) policy Triton keeps multiple versions loaded, and clients target one via `/v2/models/<name>/versions/<v>/infer`. The `latest` policy with one version (A) is the default and would serve only version 3. Version folders must be numeric, so D is invalid.

questions.q: Which set of signals is most useful for alerting on the health of a production LLM inference service?
options: Request error rate, p95/p99 latency (including TTFT), queue depth, and GPU memory/utilization
Number of model parameters and training loss
Docker image size and git commit count
BLEU score computed on every request
questions.why: These cover user-facing reliability (errors, tail latency) and leading indicators of saturation (queues, GPU memory). Reference-based scores such as BLEU (D) need ground-truth answers that live traffic does not have, so they belong in offline evaluation.

questions.q: A team serves a model with tensor parallelism of 8. They can place the 8 shards either on one 8-GPU NVSwitch node or across two 4-GPU nodes connected by Ethernet. Which choice is better and why?
options: Two nodes, because more CPUs are available
Either, because tensor parallelism communicates only once per request
Two nodes, because Ethernet has lower latency than NVLink
One NVSwitch node, because tensor parallelism performs all-reduces inside every layer and needs NVLink-class bandwidth and latency
questions.why: Tensor parallelism synchronizes activations in each transformer layer, so slow links stall every forward pass. The common rule is to keep tensor parallelism within an NVLink domain and use pipeline or data parallelism across nodes; B is wrong because communication happens many times per token, not once per request.

questions.q: A data engineer must iterate over a 2 TB dataset from the Hugging Face Hub on a machine with 500 GB of disk. Which option should they use?
options: `load_dataset(..., streaming=True)`, which returns an `IterableDataset` that reads records on the fly
`load_dataset(..., split="train[:100%]")`
`load_dataset(..., keep_in_memory=True)`
Convert the dataset to a pandas DataFrame first
questions.why: Streaming mode avoids downloading the full dataset, yielding examples as you iterate. `keep_in_memory=True` (C) does the opposite and would need even more resources than the full download.

questions.q: A team is told to prefer `.safetensors` over pickle-based `.bin`/`.pt` files when loading third-party model weights. What is the main reason?
options: Safetensors files are always smaller because they are compressed
Safetensors stores only raw tensors and metadata, so loading cannot execute arbitrary code, and it supports fast zero-copy memory mapping
Safetensors is required by CUDA
Pickle files cannot store BF16 tensors
questions.why: Unpickling can run code embedded in a malicious file, which is a supply-chain risk for downloaded weights. Safetensors is not a compression format, so A is a misconception; its size is about the same as the raw tensors.

questions.q: Which approach does PyTorch recommend for saving a trained model for later reloading in code?
options: `torch.save(model, "model.pt")` and loading the whole pickled object
Copying the Python source file next to the training logs
`torch.save(model.state_dict(), "model.pt")`, then rebuilding the model class and calling `load_state_dict`
Exporting to CSV with NumPy
questions.why: Saving the `state_dict` stores only parameter and buffer tensors, which is robust to refactoring. Pickling the whole module (A) ties the file to the exact class paths and code at save time, so it breaks easily.

questions.q: Which `nvidia-smi` query would a script use to log memory use and utilization every 5 seconds in CSV form?
options: `nvidia-smi topo -m`
`nvidia-smi -q -d ECC`
`nvidia-smi mig -lgi`
`nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,utilization.gpu --format=csv -l 5`
questions.why: `--query-gpu` selects specific fields, `--format=csv` makes the output machine-readable, and `-l 5` repeats every 5 seconds. `topo -m` (A) prints the interconnect topology matrix, not usage over time.

questions.q: Why does TensorRT's layer and tensor fusion speed up inference?
options: It removes layers whose weights are small
It combines consecutive operations (e.g., a GEMM, bias add, and activation) into one kernel, cutting kernel launches and round trips to memory for intermediate results
It increases numerical precision to FP64
It moves computation to the CPU when the GPU is busy
questions.why: Many inference layers are memory-bound, so keeping intermediate results on chip within one fused kernel saves bandwidth and launch overhead. Fusion does not change what the network computes, so it does not delete layers (A), which would be pruning.

questions.q: Why do teams often start from an NGC PyTorch container (e.g., `nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:<yy.mm>-py3`) instead of building their own image?
options: It bundles a tested, compatible set of CUDA, cuDNN, NCCL, and PyTorch versions tuned for NVIDIA GPUs and updated monthly
It contains the NVIDIA kernel driver, so no driver is needed on the host
It is the only way to use PyTorch on GPUs
It includes pretrained weights for every Hugging Face model
questions.why: NGC containers remove version-matching headaches and include NVIDIA performance tuning, with tags following a year.month release cadence. The host driver is still required (B) because containers share the host's kernel driver.

questions.q:
Load tests of a TensorRT-LLM deployment produce the following results:

| Max batch | Throughput (tok/s) | p99 inter-token latency |
|---|---|---|
| 16 | 2,400 | 28 ms |
| 32 | 3,900 | 41 ms |
| 64 | 5,100 | 72 ms |

The SLO requires p99 inter-token latency below 50 ms. Which setting should be chosen?
options: 16, because it has the lowest latency
64, because it has the highest throughput
32, the highest-throughput setting that still meets the latency SLO
48, an interpolated value that has not been tested
questions.why: The goal is the most throughput (lowest cost) subject to the SLO: 64 breaks the 50 ms limit, and 16 meets it but wastes capacity. Choosing an untested value (D) is risky; you would benchmark 48 before considering it.

questions.q:
```
dynamic_batching {
  preferred_batch_size: [ 8, 16 ]
  max_queue_delay_microseconds: 2000
}
```

What does `preferred_batch_size` tell Triton's dynamic batcher?
options: Requests with batch sizes other than 8 or 16 are rejected
The model must be loaded twice, once for each size
The client SDK must split its requests into groups of 8 or 16
The batcher should try to form batches of these sizes, sending a batch early once one is reached, otherwise falling back to the largest batch it can form when the queue delay expires
questions.why: Preferred sizes are useful when the backend runs some batch sizes especially efficiently (e.g., TensorRT optimization profiles tuned for them). Other sizes are still allowed up to `max_batch_size`, so A is wrong. For many models leaving it unset and relying on the queue delay works well.

questions.q: A streaming speech model keeps hidden state between successive audio chunks of the same utterance. Which Triton scheduler should it use?
options: The sequence batcher, which uses a correlation ID to route all requests of a sequence to the same model instance with start/end control signals
The dynamic batcher with a large queue delay
The default scheduler with several instances
An ensemble with a cache step
questions.why: Stateful models need every chunk of a sequence to reach the instance holding that sequence's state; the dynamic batcher (B) assumes requests are independent and can send them to any instance.

questions.q: A Python-backend model in Triton must send each generated token back as a separate response to one request. Which configuration enables this?
options: `max_batch_size: 0`
`instance_group { kind: KIND_CPU }`
`model_transaction_policy { decoupled: true }`, letting the model send zero or more responses per request (consumed via gRPC streaming or the generate-stream endpoint)
`sequence_batching { }`
questions.why: By default Triton expects exactly one response per request; decoupled mode breaks that link, which is what token streaming needs. The sequence batcher (D) handles state across multiple requests, not multiple responses to one request.

questions.q: A team wants to find the combination of instance count, max batch size, and dynamic batching settings that maximizes throughput while keeping p99 latency under 100 ms for a Triton model. Which tool automates this search?
options: `trtexec`
Triton Model Analyzer
Nsight Compute
`nvidia-smi dmon`
questions.why: Model Analyzer sweeps model configurations, measures them using Perf Analyzer, and reports the best ones under constraints such as latency or GPU memory. `trtexec` (A) benchmarks a single TensorRT engine but does not explore Triton server configurations.

questions.q:
Perf Analyzer is run at increasing client concurrency:

| Concurrency | Throughput (infer/s) | p95 latency |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 180 | 6 ms |
| 4 | 640 | 7 ms |
| 8 | 910 | 9 ms |
| 16 | 950 | 17 ms |
| 32 | 960 | 34 ms |

What does this curve indicate?
options: The server is CPU-bound at concurrency 1
Latency is independent of load
Doubling concurrency always doubles throughput
The server saturates around concurrency 8 to 16; beyond that, extra concurrency only adds queuing latency without meaningful throughput gains
questions.why: Throughput flattens near 950 infer/s while latency roughly doubles with each doubling of concurrency, the classic sign of saturation. The early points show near-linear scaling, which is why C is tempting, but that pattern breaks once the server is full.

questions.q: A team enables Triton's response cache for an LLM that uses temperature 0.8 sampling and sees almost no hits. Why?
options: The response cache only works for TensorRT models
The cache must be warmed for 24 hours
The cache is keyed on the exact request inputs, so it only helps when identical requests repeat, and returning cached outputs would also remove the variety expected from sampling
The response cache stores KV-cache blocks, not responses
questions.why: The response cache hashes the inputs and returns a stored response for exact repeats, which suits deterministic models with repetitive inputs (e.g., embeddings of popular queries). Option D confuses it with KV-cache reuse inside the LLM engine.

questions.q: A pipeline must call a small classifier, then call one of two different LLMs depending on the predicted class, and loop until a validation model accepts the output. What is the best Triton mechanism?
options: Business Logic Scripting (BLS) in a Python-backend model, which can call other Triton models with conditionals and loops
A standard ensemble model
Two separate Triton servers behind a load balancer
The sequence batcher
questions.why: Ensembles describe a static DAG of steps, so they cannot branch on data or loop. BLS lets Python code issue inference requests to other loaded models and implement arbitrary control flow on the server.

questions.q: A TensorRT engine for a transformer must accept sequence lengths from 1 to 2,048, with most traffic around 256 tokens. How should the build be configured?
options: Build with a fixed shape of 2,048 and pad every input
Build one engine per possible length
Set the batch size to 2,048
Define an optimization profile with min = 1, opt = 256, and max = 2,048 for the sequence dimension, so kernels are tuned for the common shape while the full range stays valid
questions.why: Optimization profiles declare the valid range of each dynamic dimension and the shape to tune for. Padding everything to 2,048 (A) works but wastes compute on most requests.

questions.q: While building a TensorRT engine from ONNX, the parser reports a custom operator that TensorRT does not support. What is the standard remedy, short of changing the model?
options: Run the whole model in FP32
Implement (or reuse) a TensorRT plugin for the op and register it so the parser and builder can include it
Delete the operator from the ONNX graph
Increase the builder workspace size
questions.why: Plugins are custom layer implementations (typically CUDA kernels) that extend TensorRT's operator set; TensorRT-LLM itself relies on plugins for some attention and GEMM paths. Deleting the operator (C) changes the model's math, and precision or workspace settings do not add operator support.

questions.q: A TensorRT-LLM engine was built with `max_seq_len` of 4,096. Product now needs 8,192-token conversations. What is required?
options: Only a change to the client's `max_tokens` parameter
Restarting Triton with a larger HTTP body limit
Rebuilding the engine with a larger maximum sequence length (if the model supports that context), and checking that enough memory remains for the larger KV cache
Enabling `preferred_batch_size`
questions.why: Build-time limits such as `max_batch_size`, `max_num_tokens`, and `max_seq_len` are baked into the engine and its memory planning. Raising the client's `max_tokens` (A) cannot exceed the engine's limits; such requests are rejected or truncated.

questions.q: A TensorRT-LLM server and a small embedding model share one GPU. After the LLM starts, the embedding model fails with out-of-memory errors. Which setting should be adjusted first?
options: Increase the LLM's `max_batch_size`
Disable in-flight batching
Switch the LLM to FP32
Lower the LLM's KV-cache free-GPU-memory fraction (e.g., `kv_cache_free_gpu_mem_fraction`) so it does not pre-allocate most of the remaining memory
questions.why: TensorRT-LLM reserves a large fraction of the free memory left after loading weights as a paged KV-cache pool, leaving little for co-located processes. Reducing that fraction (or isolating the models with MIG) frees memory at the cost of fewer concurrent sequences. Raising the batch size (A) would demand even more memory.

questions.q: A team wants to deploy FP8-quantized TensorRT-LLM engines. On which GPU will native FP8 Tensor Core execution NOT be available?
options: L40S
questions.why: FP8 Tensor Cores arrived with Ada Lovelace (e.g., L40S) and Hopper (H100) and continue in Blackwell (B200). Ampere's A100 supports TF32, BF16, FP16, INT8, and INT4 but not FP8, so INT8 or weight-only INT4 schemes are used there instead.

questions.q: Why does weight-only INT4 quantization (e.g., AWQ) typically speed up batch-size-1 token generation much more than it speeds up large-batch prefill?
options: INT4 arithmetic is used for the attention softmax

Small-batch decode is memory-bandwidth-bound on reading weights, so moving 4× fewer weight bytes helps directly, while large-batch prefill is compute-bound and weights are dequantized for higher-precision math
Prefill does not use the model weights
INT4 disables the KV cache during decode
questions.why: At small batch, each token requires streaming all the weights from HBM, so shrinking them cuts time almost proportionally. In compute-bound regimes the GEMMs still run in FP16/BF16 after dequantization, so the gain is small. Prefill certainly uses the weights (C).

questions.q: An engineer's FP32 PyTorch training on an A100 is much slower than expected, and profiling shows matmuls are not using Tensor Cores. Which one-line change enables TF32 Tensor Core math for FP32 matmuls?
options: torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False
model.half()
torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high")
torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)
questions.why: Since PyTorch 1.12, TF32 for FP32 matmuls is off by default; setting the float32 matmul precision to "high" (or torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True) lets Ampere and newer Tensor Cores run them with FP32 accumulation. model.half() also uses Tensor Cores, but it converts the weights to FP16, a larger change with different numerical risks.

questions.q: A model too large for one 8-GPU node is served across two nodes linked by InfiniBand. Which layout is usually preferred?
options: Tensor parallelism 16 across both nodes
Data parallelism 16 with a full model copy per GPU
Expert parallelism only, with no other sharding
Tensor parallelism 8 within each node and pipeline parallelism 2 across nodes
questions.why: Pipeline parallelism only passes activations between stages at layer boundaries, which tolerates the slower inter-node link, while tensor parallelism's per-layer all-reduces stay on NVLink. TP=16 across nodes (A) puts the most communication-heavy traffic on the slowest link.

questions.q: On an A100 80GB, what is the maximum number of `1g.10gb` MIG instances that can be created?
questions.why: A100 supports at most seven GPU instances; the 1g profile gets one of seven compute slices and one-eighth of memory (10 GB on the 80 GB card). The tempting answer 8 comes from 80 ÷ 10, but the compute-slice limit of 7 is binding.

questions.q: A cluster admin enables GPU time-slicing so four pods share one GPU. Which risk does this introduce compared with MIG?
options: Pods cannot use CUDA at all
The GPU's memory capacity is divided into four hard partitions
There is no memory or fault isolation, so one pod can exhaust GPU memory or degrade the others' latency
Only one pod can be scheduled on the node
questions.why: Time-slicing interleaves workloads on the same GPU but does not partition memory or SMs. Hard partitioning (B) is exactly what MIG provides and time-slicing lacks.

questions.q: What does the CUDA Multi-Process Service (MPS) enable?
options: Kernels from multiple processes can run concurrently on one GPU through a shared server context, improving utilization for small workloads, but with weaker isolation than MIG
One process can use GPUs in multiple nodes as if they were local
Hardware partitioning of memory into isolated slices
