Automatic mixed precision for multi-process training
questions.why: Without MPS, contexts from different processes are time-sliced; MPS funnels them through one server so their kernels can overlap. Hardware memory partitioning (C) is MIG's role, not MPS's.

questions.q:
```python
start = time.time()
y = model(x)            # x and model on CUDA
elapsed = time.time() - start
```

The measured time is suspiciously tiny. Why, and what is the fix?
options: `time.time()` cannot measure under one second; use `time.sleep`
The model ran on the CPU; call `.cuda()` again
Python caches the result of `model(x)`; change the input each time
CUDA kernels launch asynchronously, so the call returns before the GPU finishes; call `torch.cuda.synchronize()` before reading the clock (or use CUDA events) and add warm-up iterations
questions.why: The host only enqueues work, so without synchronization you measure launch time, not execution. Warm-up excludes one-time costs such as cuDNN autotuning or `torch.compile` compilation. PyTorch does not cache forward results (C).

questions.q: A service wraps its model with `torch.compile` and sees periodic multi-second latency spikes whenever a new input length arrives. What is the most likely cause and mitigation?
options: Garbage collection; disable Python GC
Shape changes trigger recompilation; mark dimensions dynamic (e.g., `dynamic=True`) or bucket/pad inputs to a few fixed lengths and warm them up
cuDNN is downloading kernels from the internet; pre-download them
The GPU is throttling; lower the clock speed
questions.why: TorchDynamo guards on input properties, and new shapes can invalidate guards and trigger a fresh compile. Dynamic shapes or a small set of pre-warmed buckets avoid compiling on the request path. Python GC pauses (A) are far shorter than multi-second compiles.

questions.q: Why do LLM inference engines often capture the decode step with CUDA Graphs?
options: To reduce the model's parameter count
To store the KV cache in host memory
To replay a fixed sequence of many small kernels with a single launch, removing per-kernel CPU launch overhead that dominates small-batch decode
To enable automatic mixed precision
questions.why: Each decode step runs hundreds of short kernels, and CPU launch latency can leave the GPU idle between them. A captured graph is launched as one unit, though it requires static shapes, so engines capture graphs for a set of batch sizes.

questions.q:
```python
for batch in loader:          # DataLoader(pin_memory=True)
    x = batch.to("cuda", non_blocking=True)
    out = model(x)
```

What do `pin_memory=True` and `non_blocking=True` achieve together?
options: Host-to-device copies from page-locked memory run asynchronously, so data transfer can overlap with GPU computation
The batch is compressed before transfer
The tensor is copied to every GPU
The data stays on the CPU and is read by the GPU lazily
questions.why: Asynchronous DMA transfers require pinned (page-locked) host memory; with pageable memory `non_blocking` gives little benefit. Option D describes unified/zero-copy access, which is a different mechanism.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a component that the NVIDIA GPU Operator deploys and manages?
options: NVIDIA Kubernetes device plugin
DCGM Exporter
NVIDIA Container Toolkit
Triton Inference Server
questions.why: The GPU Operator manages node-level enablement: driver, container toolkit, device plugin, GPU feature discovery, DCGM Exporter, and MIG manager. Triton is an application workload you deploy on top of GPU-ready nodes, for example with a Helm chart.

questions.q: An LLM deployment autoscales on GPU utilization, but it adds replicas too late and users see long queues. Which signal usually tracks LLM load better?
options: CPU utilization of the pods
Container image pull time
Pending/queued requests or KV-cache utilization per replica (e.g., exported by the inference server)
GPU temperature
questions.why: GPU-Util saturates near 100% at modest load (it only measures whether a kernel is running), so it stops tracking demand. Queue depth and KV-cache occupancy directly reflect how close a replica is to its concurrency limit. CPU utilization (A) is mostly irrelevant for GPU-bound serving.

questions.q: A team configures an LLM service to scale to zero replicas overnight. What is the main operational cost of this choice, and a common mitigation?
options: Higher GPU memory use; mitigate with INT8

Long cold starts (pulling large images, loading weights, building or warming engines) for the first requests; mitigate with a minimum warm replica or by caching images and weights on nodes or persistent volumes
Loss of model accuracy; mitigate with fine-tuning
Higher per-token cost at peak; mitigate with spot instances
questions.why: Scaling to zero saves GPU cost but the first request may wait minutes. Accuracy (C) is unaffected by replica count.

questions.q: Plain round-robin load balancing across LLM replicas leads to some replicas having long queues while others idle. What is a better routing strategy?
options: Random routing with a fixed seed
Routing by client IP hash only
Sending all traffic to the newest replica
Least-outstanding-requests (or load/KV-cache-aware) routing, optionally preferring replicas that already hold a matching prompt prefix in cache
questions.why: LLM requests vary by orders of magnitude in cost, so equal request counts do not mean equal load. Load-aware routing balances real work, and prefix-aware routing can increase prefix-cache hits. IP hashing (B) is sticky but ignores load entirely.

questions.q: A company has 30 customer-specific LoRA adapters for the same base LLM. What is the most GPU-efficient way to serve them with an inference stack that supports it (e.g., LLM NIM or TensorRT-LLM)?
options: Load one base model and serve the adapters dynamically, selecting the adapter per request, so different adapters can share a batch
Merge each adapter into a full copy of the model and run 30 deployments
Retrain one model on all customers' data
Run each adapter on a separate MIG instance with its own base model copy
questions.why: Adapters are small, so keeping one base copy plus many adapters uses far less memory than 30 merged models (B) and keeps the GPU busy with mixed batches. Merged per-customer deployments make sense only when traffic per adapter is very high or latency overhead must be zero.

questions.q: DCGM reports a growing count of uncorrectable ECC errors and Xid errors on one GPU in a serving node, and requests routed there intermittently fail. What is the appropriate operational response?
options: Increase `max_queue_delay_microseconds`
Lower the model's precision to INT8
Cordon and drain the node (or remove the GPU from service), then run diagnostics such as DCGM diagnostics and arrange repair or replacement
Restart only the client application
questions.why: Uncorrectable memory errors indicate a hardware fault that software tuning cannot fix, and leaving the node in rotation keeps producing failures. Changing precision (B) does not repair faulty memory.

questions.q: A multi-node job hangs at the first all-reduce. Which first step gives the most useful diagnostic information?
options: Reduce the learning rate
Switch from BF16 to FP32
Increase `num_workers` on the DataLoader
Rerun with `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` to log the transports, network interfaces, and topology NCCL selects, then check interface selection and firewall/IB connectivity
questions.why: Hangs at the first collective are usually connectivity or interface-selection problems (e.g., NCCL choosing an unreachable interface, fixable via `NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME`). Numerical settings such as precision (B) do not affect whether ranks can connect.

questions.q: What does GPUDirect RDMA provide in a multi-node GPU cluster?
options: A way to run CUDA kernels on the network adapter
Direct data transfer between GPU memory and the network adapter (e.g., InfiniBand), bypassing a copy through host memory
Compression of gradients before they are sent
A replacement for NVLink inside a node
questions.why: Removing the bounce through CPU memory cuts latency and CPU overhead for inter-node collectives. It complements NVLink rather than replacing it (D); NVLink handles intra-node GPU traffic.

options: ONNX Runtime evaluates the `if` and calls `self.b`
Export fails with an error
The exported graph only contains the branch taken during tracing, so `self.a` runs for every input
Both branches run and their outputs are averaged
questions.why: Tracing records the operations executed for the example input, so data-dependent Python control flow is frozen (usually with a tracer warning). Preserving it needs scripting, rewriting with tensor ops such as `torch.where`, or the newer dynamo-based exporter that captures control flow explicitly.

questions.q: A Triton model config sets `max_batch_size: 0` with input `dims: [ 4, 128 ]`. What does this mean?
options: Triton does not add an implicit batch dimension or batch requests for this model; each request must provide exactly a `[4, 128]` tensor, whose first dimension the model may treat as its own batch
The model is disabled
Triton will choose the batch size automatically
The model accepts any batch size up to 128
questions.why: With `max_batch_size: 0` the `dims` are the full tensor shape and Triton's batchers cannot combine requests. Models that batch internally (or handle batching themselves, like some LLM backends) often use this setting. It does not disable the model (B).

questions.q: A model has 32 layers, 8 KV heads, and head dimension 128, and its KV cache is stored in FP16. After loading weights, 40 GB of GPU memory is available for KV cache. Roughly how many concurrent 4,096-token sequences fit?
options: About 10
About 20
About 320
About 80
questions.why: Per token: 2 (K and V) × 32 layers × 8 heads × 128 × 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB. A 4,096-token sequence needs 4,096 × 128 KiB = 512 MiB, so 40 GB ÷ 0.5 GB ≈ 80 sequences. Forgetting the factor of 2 for K and V gives about 160, and using 32 query heads instead of 8 KV heads gives about 20 (B).

questions.q: When deploying an LLM on a Jetson Orin module, why must model weights, KV cache, and the OS fit in one memory budget?
options: Jetson has no GPU, so the model runs entirely on CPU RAM
Jetson's CPU and integrated GPU share the same physical DRAM (unified memory), so there is no separate GPU memory pool
Jetson GPUs use HBM that is reserved for graphics
Jetson streams weights from cloud storage at runtime
questions.why: On Jetson the integrated GPU and CPU use the same LPDDR memory, so OS, application, weights, and cache compete for one pool, which is why aggressive quantization and small models are common. Jetson does have a CUDA-capable GPU, so A is wrong.

questions.q: A canary receives 1% of traffic for 10 minutes, shows 0 errors versus the baseline's 0.2% error rate, and the team proposes promoting it immediately. What is the main concern?
options: The sample is too small to distinguish error rates of this size, so the canary should run longer or at higher traffic and be compared with the baseline over the same window before promotion
Canaries should never be compared with the baseline
Zero errors proves the new model is better
Error rates are irrelevant for model rollouts
questions.why: With a few hundred requests, observing zero failures is quite likely even if the true error rate equals the baseline's. Sound canary analysis needs enough traffic and a concurrent baseline so time-of-day effects cancel out; C overstates what a small sample shows.

questions.q: An operations team wants to add and update models in Triton without restarting the server, controlling exactly when each model loads. Which setup supports this?
options: `--model-control-mode=none` with a read-only repository
Restarting the pod for every update
`--model-control-mode=explicit` and calling the repository API (e.g., `POST /v2/repository/models/<name>/load`) after updating the files
Setting `max_batch_size: 0`
questions.why: In explicit mode, models load and unload only when requested through the model-control API, which allows controlled hot updates. In `none` mode (A), Triton loads everything at startup and ignores later repository changes. A `poll` mode also exists but gives less control over timing.

questions.q: A NIM streams tokens correctly when called directly, but through the company's reverse proxy the client receives the whole answer at once at the end. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model was built without streaming support
The client must use gRPC for streaming
The GPU is too slow
The proxy is buffering the response; disable response buffering for the SSE route (e.g., `proxy_buffering off` in NGINX) and keep timeouts long enough for the stream
questions.why: Because direct calls stream correctly, the server is fine; the intermediary is collecting chunks before forwarding them. Option A contradicts the direct-call evidence, and SSE over HTTP needs no gRPC (B).

questions.q: A hosted API charges $0.50 per million output tokens. Self-hosting costs $3.00 per GPU-hour for a replica with a peak capacity of 3,000 tokens/s, but traffic keeps it only 50% busy on average. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Self-hosting costs about $0.28 per million tokens, so it is cheaper
Self-hosting costs about $0.56 per million tokens at 50% utilization, so the API is slightly cheaper unless utilization rises
Self-hosting costs about $1.11 per million tokens, so the API is twice as cheap
The costs cannot be compared without knowing the model size
questions.why: At 50% utilization the replica produces 1,500 × 3,600 = 5.4 million tokens per hour, so $3.00 / 5.4 ≈ $0.56 per million. The $0.28 figure (A) assumes 100% utilization, a common mistake in cost estimates. Staffing and operations costs would add further to the self-hosted figure.
